blocks.value: **Arithmetic operators** perform basic mathematical operations on numerical values.
**Integer division** occurs when **both** operands are integers. The result is an integer, and any fractional part is lost:
**Floating-point division** occurs when **either or both** operands are floating-point values. The result is a floating-point value:
Nothing warns you about this. `11 / 3` giving `3` is not an error in Java. It is the defined behaviour, so a wrong average or a wrong percentage just quietly appears in your output.
The first line computes `7 / 10` as integer division, gets `0`, then multiplies by 100. **If you want a decimal result, at least one operand must be a decimal type.**
`%` gives the **remainder** after division. It looks like a curiosity and turns out to be everywhere:

System.out.println(11 % 3);        // 2, 3 goes into 11 three times, remainder 2
System.out.println(10 % 2);        // 0, evenly divisible
System.out.println(7 % 2);         // 1

int seconds = 3725;
System.out.println(seconds / 60);  // 62 minutes total
System.out.println(seconds % 60);  // 5 seconds left over
`n % 2 == 0` is the standard test for "is this even." You will use it constantly once you reach loops.
When either side of `+` is a `String`, it joins instead of adding. Java works left to right, so the order decides which `+` adds and which joins:

System.out.println("Total: " + 1 + 2);       // Total: 12
System.out.println(1 + 2 + " total");       // 3 total
System.out.println("Total: " + (1 + 2));     // Total: 3
In the first line, `"Total: " + 1` is already a `String` by the time `+ 2` runs, so the `2` is joined, not added. Use parentheses to add first.
